channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: Starbucks' US Sales Rose 7.7%, on Bigger Tickets, Its Strongest Fall Menu, and 250 Closed Stores
item.description: Starbucks reported US comparable sales up 7.7% in its fiscal fourth quarter — ticket size up 5.2% and transactions up 2.4%. Its fall menu launch was the strongest in the company's history, matcha is now a $1 billion line, and about 250 closed stores contributed roughly two points of the growth as their customers moved.
item.content:encoded:
Starbucks' US same-store sales rose 7.7% in its fiscal fourth quarter, the company reported on Thursday — a 5.2% increase in average ticket and 2.4% growth in transactions, according to its earnings release, covered by Restaurant Dive. Global comparable sales rose 7.2%. Adjusted earnings were 80 cents a share, above the 72 cents analysts expected; revenue fell 4% to $9.14 billion, below the $9.2 billion expected, because the company converted its China retail operations to a licensed joint venture, which changed how that revenue is reported (Associated Press). Chief executive Brian Niccol said the chain is moving from turnaround to a sustained growth plan, with sales growth broad-based across income levels, generations and dayparts.

Two details in the quarter explain where the growth came from. The fall menu launch — headlined, as every year, by the Pumpkin Spice Latte — was the strongest fall deployment in the company's history, and matcha has grown into a $1 billion product line of its own, drunk mainly in the afternoon. And about 200 basis points of the comparable-sales growth came from store closures: Starbucks closed about 250 underperforming North American coffeehouses concentrated at the end of September, and their customers shifted to the stores that remained, chief financial officer Catherine Smith told analysts. For fiscal 2027, the company expects North American comparable sales to grow about 4%, and Smith said any price increases will remain focused and well below the Consumer Price Index. The shares fell almost 2% in after-hours trading on Thursday.

item.title: The Price Held. The Amount Did Not.
item.description: OpenAI kept the number that will be quoted, a $1.25 trillion valuation, and reduced the number that will be paid: a $20 billion target, a first close expected below it, and less than half of the original $30 billion raised, the Wall Street Journal reports. The first market-set price for a frontier lab now belongs to Anthropic's November roadshow.
item.content:encoded: OpenAI kept the number that will be quoted, a $1.25 trillion valuation, and reduced the number that will be paid. The target is now $20 billion, the first close is expected below that, and the Wall Street Journal reports less than half of the original $30 billion was raised. A private valuation is a negotiated figure, and the negotiation shows its limit: the price held because the amount gave way. The first market-set price for a frontier lab now belongs to Anthropic, whose roadshow starts in the week of November 9. Until that price exists, private valuations in this sector should be read with the condition Friday attached to this one: they hold for the amount investors will actually fund.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: Polymarket Suspended International Trading After $2.6 Million Was Drained From User Accounts
item.description: Polymarket suspended international trading on Thursday after hackers drained more than $2.6 million from user accounts, CoinDesk reported — the second crypto security incident of the day, days before the midterm elections that bring prediction markets their largest audiences.
item.content:encoded:
Polymarket, the prediction-market platform, suspended international trading on Thursday after hackers drained more than $2.6 million from user accounts, CoinDesk reported on Friday. The suspension was the second crypto security incident reported on Thursday: the larger one, a $6.3 billion theft from the exchange Binance, is covered in this edition's Latest. CoinDesk's report gives the amount taken and the suspension; it does not describe how the accounts were accessed.

The timing is the part users will notice. Prediction markets take their largest public audiences in election weeks, and the US midterm elections are on Tuesday, November 3. A platform that suspends international trading days before that vote is removing, for its non-US users, the product at the moment of its highest demand — while its federally regulated rival Kalshi, covered in this edition, spent the same week raising $1 billion at a $40 billion valuation. Two platforms selling the same underlying product, event contracts, carried two different risks into election week: one regulatory and financial, one a security failure measured, so far, in single millions rather than billions.

item.title: OpenAI Cut Its Funding Target From $30 Billion to $20 Billion at a $1.25 Trillion Valuation
item.description: OpenAI cut the target for its bridge financing by a third on the day investor commitments were due, the Financial Times reported on Friday. The $1.25 trillion valuation stayed where the October talks had put it. The first close is expected to raise less than the new $20 billion target, and the Wall Street Journal reported that less than half of the original $30 billion had been raised.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI has cut the target for its new funding round from up to $30 billion to about $20 billion, the Financial Times reported on Friday, in a report carried by Reuters. The valuation is unchanged in this step at $1.25 trillion before new money. OpenAI set Friday, October 30, as the deadline for investors to commit. According to the Reuters account of the FT report, some investors reduced their allocations, and the first close of the round is expected to raise less than $20 billion. The account does not name the investors who cut back. OpenAI did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment. Later on Friday, the Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI has raised less than half of its original $30 billion target in the round.

Who is in the smaller round

The FT reported that a consortium of investors from the United Arab Emirates, including the state-backed fund MGX, is expected to be the largest participant, and that under the arrangement OpenAI would gain an option to lease newly developed computing capacity in the region. Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to participate, according to the FT report. Wealthy individuals are expected to be offered a subsequent retail offering at the same $1.25 trillion valuation. Those participation details are reported, not announced; OpenAI has made no statement about the round.

The round's path, on this paper's record

The financing has been repriced twice in five weeks. OpenAI first pitched a $1.4 trillion valuation (Edition 003). On October 22, CNBC and Bloomberg reported the valuation in talks at $1.25 trillion with up to $30 billion still sought, led by Coatue and UAE investors (Edition 003–004). Signatures were then targeted for Friday, October 30 (Editions 004–012), with some backers wanting Anthropic priced first (Edition 007) — a sequence that could not happen, since Anthropic's roadshow is scheduled for the week of November 9 (Edition 008). Friday's report resolves the collision by reducing the amount instead of waiting for the rival's price. OpenAI's last completed round, closed March 31, 2026, raised $122 billion in committed capital at an $852 billion post-money valuation, anchored by Amazon, Nvidia and SoftBank, according to the published accounts carried in Friday's coverage. The new round is described in that coverage as interim funding — a bridge toward a planned listing in the first half of 2027.

The cut landed on the week's hardest day for the sector's public prices. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% on Friday (see Latest), and after the close S&P Global Ratings turned its outlook on Meta negative, citing uncertainty over how long Meta's heavy capital spending will last, according to a summary of the action. Anthropic's roadshow, in the week of November 9, will now produce the first price for a frontier lab that a public market has set. OpenAI's $1.25 trillion remains a negotiated figure: agreed for the smaller amount investors funded on Friday, and untested at the $30 billion size at which it was first offered.

item.title: October Ended With the Bill Marked in Public
item.description: The month that opened with a $1.4 trillion pitch closed with three public tests of what AI claims are worth: a private round that defended its price by shrinking its size, an earnings season that marked down named balance sheets one at a time, and a $6.3 billion theft absorbed by a promise to cover it.
item.content:encoded:
October opened, on this paper's record, with a pitch: OpenAI seeking $1.4 trillion (Edition 003). It closed on Friday with three separate tests of what claims on the AI buildout are worth, each run in a different venue. In the private market, OpenAI defended the $1.25 trillion valuation its talks had settled on and cut the amount from $30 billion to $20 billion, with less than that expected at the first close (the Lead). In the public market, an earnings season that established demand — Azure up 48%, Google Cloud up 103%, AWS up 39% (Editions 011–012) — ended with the cash-flow test applied across the chip sector at once: Intel down 28.58% on guidance, the Nasdaq down 2.86% on the day and 5.3% on the month, while six of the S&P 500's eleven sectors rose (see Latest). In crypto, a $6.3 billion theft from the largest exchange was met with a freeze of about half the assets and a pledge to cover the rest, and bitcoin, after falling to $76,400, ended the day above $76,700.

Read together, the three tests drew the same line in three places. What held was the price attached to the established thing: OpenAI's valuation, the wider stock index, the value of a bitcoin. What gave way was the quantity attached to the promise: the size of the round funded on Friday, the fourth-quarter revenue Intel would commit to, the share of the stolen assets that could actually be frozen. October's repricing, in other words, has not been a repricing of the present. Demand for cloud capacity printed at record levels all month, the memory suppliers' order books sold out into 2027, and 82% of reporting S&P 500 companies beat estimates. The repricing has been applied to the next tranche — the unfunded part of every plan.

The financing record shows the same split from the lenders' side. Alphabet raised $147.2 billion from outside investors in the first nine months of the year (Edition 011). Amazon's long-term debt reached $173.1 billion (Edition 012). After Friday's close, S&P Global Ratings moved its outlook on Meta — which priced a $97.5 billion equity program on Tuesday (Edition 009) — to negative, citing uncertainty about how long the heavy spending lasts. None of those facts establishes that the spending fails. They establish that each new layer of it is being examined separately, at its own price, rather than carried on the strength of the layers beneath it. Two-tier money (Edition 007) has become the ordinary condition, not the warning.

November supplies the missing benchmark. On Monday, Apple and Palantir report, testing whether Friday's selloff stays inside the chip supply chain. On Tuesday, the midterm elections price the political environment the buildout's permits, power contracts and export rules will be written in. By Wednesday, Moonshot's Kimi weights are due — an open test of whether the frontier's capability claims can be checked by anyone with the file. And in the week of November 9, Anthropic's roadshow sets the first public price for a frontier lab, against a filed prospectus whose figures the market has now had two weeks to read. Every private number in this sector, including Friday's defended $1.25 trillion, will be quoted against that price from then on.

item.title: The Nasdaq Fell 2.86% on Friday, and Intel Fell 28.6% in Its Worst Day Since the 1970s
item.description: The Nasdaq Composite fell 747.72 points to 25,437.00 and the S&P 500 fell 1.82% in its worst session since June, as Intel fell 28.58% a day after guiding the fourth quarter below expectations. The selling stayed inside the chip sector: six of the S&P 500's eleven sectors rose, and the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.93%.
item.content:encoded:
US stocks closed sharply lower on Friday, October 30. The Nasdaq Composite fell 747.72 points, or 2.86%, to 25,437.00 — its lowest finish since July 31 — the S&P 500 lost 140.32 points, or 1.82%, to 7,580.07 in its worst session since June, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31 (Market Briefer, from exchange close reports). Intel fell 28.58% to $65.76, in what CNBC described as its worst session since the 1970s, a day after its fourth-quarter guidance came in below expectations (Edition 012). The semiconductor selloff took the Nasdaq 100 down 3.46% and a large semiconductor ETF down more than 8%; Qualcomm fell 11.12%, Nvidia fell 4.22%, Advanced Micro Devices and Marvell fell by double digits, and Broadcom and Micron each lost more than 5%. Technology was the S&P 500's weakest sector, down 4.24%. Amazon, which also reported Thursday night, fell 1.41%.

Outside the chip sector, the session was orderly. Six of the S&P 500's eleven sectors rose, led by energy, up 1.91%, and consumer staples, up 1.38%; utilities, health care, real estate and materials also finished higher. The Russell 2000 fell 1.66% to 2,811.84, and the Cboe Volatility Index rose to 19.42. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.93% from 4.98%, ending October down roughly 36 basis points — its largest monthly decline since December 2023, according to the Wall Street Journal, as reported by Market Briefer. Gold fell 3.63% to $3,884.90 an ounce, its lowest level in about a year. The morning's labor data added nothing to either case: the third-quarter Employment Cost Index rose 0.8%, in line with expectations (Bureau of Labor Statistics). Of the 299 S&P 500 companies that had reported third-quarter results through Friday, 82% beat consensus estimates, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.

For the month, the Nasdaq fell 5.3% — its largest monthly decline since March 2025 — and now sits more than 8% below its record closing high of October 6. The S&P 500 fell 0.9% in October while the Dow added 1.7%. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq have now fallen for three straight weeks. Friday's session applied, to the whole chip sector at once, the test Thursday's session had applied to Alphabet alone (Edition 012): earnings that beat estimates did not protect a company whose outlook showed the spending continuing. The difference on Friday is that the test had a named trigger — one company's guidance — and the rest of the market, and the bond market, declined to follow it.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Kalshi Raised $1 Billion at a $40 Billion Valuation, Its Second $1 Billion Round in Five Months
item.description: Kalshi, the federally regulated prediction-market exchange, closed a $1 billion Series G co-led by Wellington Management and Sequoia Capital at a $40 billion post-money valuation. The company says annualized trading volume exceeds $1 trillion. Its sports contracts remain under legal challenge from state authorities.
item.content:encoded:
Kalshi announced a $1 billion Series G financing on October 29, in a company post reported by Crunchbase News on October 30. The round was co-led by Wellington Management and Sequoia Capital and values the company at $40 billion after the new money. Other participants include Baillie Gifford, Stripes, Andreessen Horowitz, Coatue, Layer Global, Morgan Stanley Investment Management, Sequoia Global Equities, CapitalG, Hudson River Trading and Balyasny Asset Management. The round follows a $1 billion raise about five months earlier at a $22 billion valuation.

Kalshi operates a federally regulated exchange in the United States for event contracts — contracts that pay out depending on whether a stated event happens. The company says its annualized trading volume now exceeds $1 trillion, that it accounts for more than 75% of prediction-market trading volume, and that its non-sports revenue exceeds $1 billion on an annualized basis; those figures are the company's. It plans to use the new capital for product development, its institutional business and international expansion, and, according to reports of its plans, for new products including leveraged event contracts, perpetual futures on individual stocks, and markets based on compute prices.

The valuation prices two things at once. The first is volume: a market that began with political and economic events now runs, by the company's own count, at a trillion-dollar annualized pace, with sports contracts a large part of it. The second is a legal position. Kalshi's sports-related contracts have drawn challenges from state authorities, who allege some offerings amount to unauthorized gambling; Kalshi disputes that reading and operates under federal derivatives regulation through the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The company's founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, started Kalshi in 2018. The round was announced in the week before the November 3 midterm elections, one of the periods when event contracts draw their widest public attention.

item.title: Halloween Spending Reaches a Record $13.5 Billion, and the Candy Bag Costs 71% More Than in 2021
item.description: The National Retail Federation expects record Halloween spending of $13.5 billion, an average of $115.14 per person celebrating. Costumes take $4.4 billion, decorations $4.3 billion and candy $4.1 billion. A 100-piece bag of assorted candy averages $16.96, up 71% since 2021.
item.content:encoded:
Americans are expected to spend $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, a record, according to the National Retail Federation's annual survey — up from $13.1 billion in 2025, at an average of $115.14 per person celebrating, against $114.45 last year. The survey, conducted by Prosper Insights & Analytics among 7,889 adults from September 1 to 9, splits the spending nearly evenly: costumes $4.4 billion (including $2 billion for adults, $1.5 billion for children and $920 million for pets), decorations $4.3 billion and candy $4.1 billion, with greeting cards adding $0.8 billion. About 74% of consumers plan to celebrate; the most common activities are handing out candy (61%), dressing in costume (50%), and a tie among decorating, carving pumpkins and watching scary movies (42% each). Spider-Man is the leading children's costume, with 4.6 million children planning to wear it.

The candy line carries the price story. A 100-piece bag of assorted Halloween candy averages $16.96 this year, according to a FinanceBuzz study reported by Stacker — up about 3.5% from $16.39 in 2025, and up 71% from $9.91 in 2021. Candy is also the purchase almost nobody skips: 96% of Halloween shoppers plan to buy it, against 78% buying decorations and 71% buying costumes. The arithmetic of the holiday, for the households handing it out tonight, is that the one item bought fresh every year is the one whose price has risen fastest — while the record total is reached by spending slightly more per person across everything else.

item.title: Four Rival AI Labs Agreed to Honor One Line That Opts a Website Out of Training
item.description: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic said on Friday they will all honor a single robots.txt token, __usage_ai-training, so a publisher can refuse training use by all four crawlers with one entry. The signal covers training only, not fetching, and does not remove material already collected.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic said on October 30 that they will all honor a single robots.txt policy token, __usage_ai-training, so a website can opt its content out of AI training by all four companies' crawlers with one entry, The Verge reported. The mechanism sits in the file site owners already use to direct crawlers: a User-Agent line naming the token, followed by Disallow or Allow lines that carve out exceptions.

The scope is narrower than the headline suggests, and the reporting states the limits plainly. The token governs training use; it is not a directive about crawling or fetching, so it does not by itself stop a crawler from reading a page for search or for answering a user's question. Updating robots.txt does not remove material already collected into existing datasets or models. The document behind the announcement is an individual IETF Internet-Draft titled "Machine-Readable Training Preference Signal," written by Anthropic's Kevin Kelley and dated October 30, 2026; the IETF's own tracker notes that an individual draft is not endorsed by the IETF and has no formal standing in the standards process.

The timelines differ by company. Anthropic says it has already begun implementing the signal. OpenAI says it aims to implement it in the coming months. Microsoft targets February 1, 2027, and Google says 2027. For publishers, the practical change is administrative: one line in one file, maintained once, replaces separate opt-out mechanisms for each of the four largest Western AI labs — provided the companies implement it on the schedules they have stated, which readers can check against the dates above.

item.title: Foundry Robotics Raised $100 Million to Build a Factory That Switches Products Without Retooling
item.description: Foundry Robotics closed a $100 million Series A led by Marlinspike Partners to expand a 130,000-square-foot factory in Emeryville, California. Its robotic cells are reconfigured by software between products — drones, underwater vehicles, satellites, ground robots and data-center equipment — instead of being rebuilt for each one.
item.content:encoded:
Foundry Robotics has raised $100 million in an oversubscribed Series A round led by Marlinspike Partners, with Khosla Ventures, SE Ventures and Wing VC among the participants. The company will use the money to expand a 130,000-square-foot facility in Emeryville, California, to develop its robotics further and to recruit. Foundry says its manufacturing footprint has increased twentyfold; that figure is the company's.

The company's product is the factory itself. Conventional assembly lines are built for one product and rebuilt — at cost, over months — when the product changes. Foundry's system uses AI-controlled robotic cells that can be reconfigured for different manufacturing tasks, coordinated by its FoundryOS software across the factory floor and cloud systems; data from each assembly run feeds back into the models that run the next one. The company is targeting a specific bottleneck: US defense contractors and industrial hardware producers that need drones, underwater vehicles, satellites, ground robots and data-center equipment in volumes their existing suppliers cannot easily expand to meet.

Foundry was founded by Adarsh Kulkarni and Emmanuel Lamacchia, a former Tesla manufacturing executive. What the announcement does not contain is the operating record: the company has not disclosed production volumes, customer contract values, or independently verified productivity figures, and the coverage of the round notes that absence. The claim being funded is therefore a capacity claim — that software-reconfigurable cells remove the retooling cost that makes small and medium production runs expensive — and the Emeryville expansion is the test of it: a factory twenty times larger either produces across several product lines without retooling, or it becomes a larger version of the conventional plant it set out to replace.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: Crushed Shells Mixed Into Beach Sand Helped Young Clams Grow in More Acidic Water
item.description: Adding shell fragments to the sand where baby clams burrow changed the water between the grains, lowered its acidity, and produced larger shells — a measured version of a shell-adding practice Indigenous communities have used for generations.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: A Structure Called the Cat’s Tail Records a Pluto-Scale Collision 63 Light-Years Away
item.description: Hubble has imaged the Cat’s Tail in visible light for the first time: a dark stream about 1,000 times the Earth–Sun distance across, inside a young star’s debris disk — evidence of a collision between bodies the size of Pluto.

item.title: Hackers Took $6.3 Billion From Binance in About 20 Minutes, the Largest Crypto Theft on Record
item.description: Binance, the largest crypto exchange, said about $6.3 billion was taken from its hot wallets on Thursday across 10 blockchains. Analytics firms attribute the theft to a North Korea-linked group. About $3 billion has been frozen with partners, withdrawals are paused, and Binance says it will cover every loss.
item.content:encoded:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said on Thursday that a security incident had affected about $6.3 billion of crypto assets — more than four times the $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025, the previous largest theft on record. According to TRM Labs, the attacker moved about $6.36 billion across 10 blockchains in roughly 20 minutes, starting Thursday afternoon Eastern time. Blockchain analytics firm Arkham Intelligence reported that 70 wallet addresses believed to belong to the attackers held a combined $5.788 billion as of Friday afternoon, including 1.768 billion Tether (USDT), 18,270 bitcoin, 497,976 ether and about 824.6 million USD Coin (USDC) (Seoul Economic Daily, reporting Arkham's figures).

TRM Labs and Elliptic attribute the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korea-linked hacking group; Binance itself has not named an attacker. Binance said its initial investigation indicated the attacker compromised an engineer's laptop, gained access to the environment running internal services, and executed unauthorized withdrawals. In an update on Friday, the exchange said investigators had found additional points of breach beyond the laptop, that the unauthorized outflows had stopped, and that the full attack path remains under investigation.

The response so far is a freeze and a pledge. Binance said about $3 billion of the assets have been frozen together with partner firms: Tether's chief executive Paolo Ardoino said the company had frozen more than $1.567 billion of USDT linked to the incident, and Circle's Jeremy Allaire said Circle had frozen more than $800 million of USDC (CoinDesk). Binance has reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds to cover losses, including $5 billion already held in the affected tokens, according to its updates on X, and co-chief executive Richard Teng posted that user money is safe and the exchange is covering every loss. Withdrawals remain paused while the exchange rebuilds its withdrawal system; deposits are working again. Bitcoin fell to a low of $76,400 on Friday, its lowest since September 18, and crypto futures liquidations reached $1.57 billion, most of them bets on rising prices (CoinDesk). The frozen half of the theft is mostly stablecoins, which issuers can freeze; the bitcoin portion, as hardware-wallet company Ballet's Bobby Lee noted in Friday coverage, is the part least likely to be recoverable.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.

item.title: Spotify Plans to Charge $4 to $5 Extra for an AI Remix Service, the FT Reports
item.description: The service, reported to be planned for the first quarter of 2027, would let subscribers remake songs with AI — a folk track as a dance track, or one artist covering another. Spotify has licensing deals with Universal, Merlin and Believe, and is still negotiating with Sony and Warner, the FT reported via Reuters.
item.content:encoded:
Spotify plans to launch an AI music remix service in the first quarter of 2027, the Financial Times reported on Friday, in a report carried by Reuters. The service would let subscribers use AI to make their own versions of songs — turning a folk song into a dance track, or making one artist appear to cover another's song — for an additional $4 to $5 a month, according to the report. Spotify did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment, and the timing is reported to target an unveiling around the Grammy Awards in February.

The licensing is the substance of the story. The FT reported that Spotify has reached deals with Universal Music Group, the independent label group Merlin and the French company Believe, and is still negotiating with Sony Music and Warner Music. A remix feature built on licensed catalogues is a different product from the unlicensed AI covers that have circulated online for two years: the labels are being paid before the feature exists, and the two largest remaining catalogues are the price of completing it. Whether listeners will pay a second monthly fee, on top of a subscription, to remake songs they already stream is the consumer question the 2027 launch will answer.

item.title: Samsung's Operating Profit Hit a Record 107.4 Trillion Won, Almost All of It From Chips
item.description: Samsung confirmed third-quarter operating profit of 107.4 trillion won, the first quarter above 100 trillion won for any technology company. Its chip division earned 106.5 trillion won of it; the division that makes its phones and appliances lost money for a second straight quarter.
item.content:encoded:
Samsung Electronics confirmed its full third-quarter results on Thursday in Seoul. Revenue was 195.25 trillion won and operating profit was 107.44 trillion won — about $80 billion — up roughly ninefold from a year earlier and 20% from the second quarter. Samsung is the first technology company to report operating profit above 100 trillion won in a single quarter. Both figures matched the preliminary guidance the company issued on October 8; the new information in Thursday's report is the division breakdown and the outlook given on the earnings call.

The Device Solutions division — memory, chip design and foundry — earned 106.5 trillion won of operating profit on 147.1 trillion won of revenue, about 99% of the company's total. Memory revenue was 140.7 trillion won, up 427% year over year. Samsung said sales of HBM4, its newest high-bandwidth memory, more than tripled from the second quarter and made up 60% of its HBM sales, and that average DRAM selling prices rose about 20% in the quarter. Jaejune Kim, the executive vice president for memory sales and marketing, told analysts that Samsung's 2027 HBM supply is already sold out. The Device eXperience division — phones, televisions and appliances — posted an operating loss of 800 billion won, its second consecutive quarterly loss, as the memory prices that enrich the chip division raise its own component costs.

Samsung approved a third-quarter dividend of 30 trillion won and said full-year capital spending will be about 84.4 trillion won, most of it in the chip division. It expects AI-related memory demand to grow faster than supply in 2027. Samsung shares fell 5.48% in Seoul on Thursday despite the record result. The division split is the week's supplier story in one company: the same memory shortage is a record profit on one side of Samsung and a loss on the other.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: Opentrons Raised $40 Million to Put AI-Driven Laboratory Robots in More Labs
item.description: Opentrons builds open, programmable robots that run laboratory experiments, and says more than 11,000 of them are deployed in over 80 countries. The $40 million Series E, led by Avego, funds the software and data layer that lets AI systems design, run and revise experiments in a continuous loop.
item.content:encoded:
Opentrons Labworks announced a $40 million Series E financing on Thursday, led by the healthcare investor Avego with participation from BroadOak Capital Partners. Existing investors include SoftBank Vision Fund and Khosla Ventures. The company, founded in 2014 and based in Long Island City, New York, is led by chief executive James Atwood. It did not disclose a valuation.

Opentrons builds laboratory robots — the Flex platform — that are open and programmable through an API, so experiments can be specified in software, run by the robot, and repeated identically in another laboratory. The company says more than 11,000 of its robots are deployed in laboratories in over 80 countries, including at 90% of the top 20 global pharmaceutical companies and every top-15 US research university. Those deployment figures are the company's. The new capital goes to scaling its robotics, software and data infrastructure, to AI-driven experimental execution, and to expansion into new markets.

The company's stated problem is a sequencing gap in AI-driven science: frontier models can now generate hypotheses and design experiments faster than physical laboratories can run them, so the bottleneck moves from the model to the bench. Opentrons' answer is to make the bench programmable — each experiment run on its robots produces structured, reproducible data that the next round of model work can use. The round lands in a competitive stretch for laboratory automation: the British company Automata raised $45 million in February, and Multiply Labs raised $75 million this month for robotic biomanufacturing (Dealroom). What distinguishes the claims here is installed base: Opentrons is selling an execution layer on top of 11,000 machines already in laboratories, not asking laboratories to adopt a first machine.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: Microsoft Booked $10 Billion in Revenue From OpenAI in One Quarter, Its Filing Shows
item.description: Microsoft's quarterly filing discloses $10.0 billion of revenue from its commercial arrangements with OpenAI in the three months to September 30 — nearly 11% of its total revenue — and $7.2 billion of receivables from OpenAI at quarter-end, up from $6.0 billion in June.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft's Form 10-Q, filed this week, discloses $10.0 billion of revenue from its commercial arrangements with OpenAI in the three months ended September 30, including revenue-sharing payments (TechCrunch, reading the filing). The figure is nearly 11% of Microsoft's $92.3 billion of quarterly revenue (Edition 011). Revenue from OpenAI for the full fiscal year to June 2026 was $24.1 billion. Microsoft did not break the $10 billion down between Azure cloud services and revenue sharing.

The same filing puts accounts receivable from OpenAI at $7.2 billion on September 30, up from $6.0 billion on June 30. Receivables are amounts owed for past transactions; they are not additional revenue, and the filing does not say why the balance grew. Microsoft holds an approximately 24% interest in OpenAI on an as-converted basis, down from about 25% in June, and reports $13.0 billion of funding commitments to OpenAI, of which $12.0 billion had been funded by September 30.

The disclosure matters because of where it sits. The $10 billion appears in the quarterly filing's related-party notes, not in the earnings release that carried the quarter's headlines. One customer — a company Microsoft part-owns, funds, and supplies — now accounts for about a ninth of its revenue, and the document that establishes the figure is the filing, read after the earnings call. OpenAI's bridge signatures are due today; what its largest partner's books show is part of the evidence those signatures are written against.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Intel Beat Third-Quarter Estimates, Then Guided the Fourth Quarter Well Below Them
item.description: Intel's third-quarter revenue rose 21% to $16.5 billion and adjusted earnings of 52 cents a share beat the 40 cents expected, with data-center and AI revenue up 78%. The fourth-quarter guide — revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion against $17.1 billion expected — sent the shares down sharply after hours.
item.content:encoded:
Intel reported third-quarter results after Thursday's close. Revenue rose 21% year over year to $16.51 billion, in line with the $16.5 billion consensus compiled by LSEG. Adjusted earnings were 52 cents a share, against 40 cents expected, and adjusted gross margin was 44.1%, above the company's 42% guidance. Intel said it was the eighth consecutive quarter in which revenue, gross margin and earnings beat its own guidance. Data Center and AI revenue rose 78% to $7.3 billion. Client Computing and Physical AI revenue fell 5% to $8.1 billion; Intel attributed the weakness to industry-wide memory shortages raising PC component prices and to limited customer IT budgets.

The fourth-quarter guidance reversed the response. Intel forecast revenue of $15.0 billion to $16.0 billion and adjusted earnings of 25 cents a share, against analyst expectations of about $17.1 billion and 43 cents, with adjusted gross margin of 38%. Shares fell more than 16% in extended trading; some market reports put the after-hours decline near 23%. Intel said total capital spending for 2026 will remain about $20 billion and rise significantly in 2027 to expand manufacturing capacity for AI server CPUs. Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner said 2027 will be an investment year in which the company may not achieve positive free cash flow.

Intel's quarter is the supplier side of this week's results read from the other end. The memory makers — SK Hynix (Edition 011) and Samsung, in this edition — reported record margins because memory is scarce. Intel's client business is one of the buyers paying for that scarcity, in a quarter when its data-center business grew at its fastest rate in 15 years on the same AI demand.

item.title: Google's AI Search Would Not Say Who Won the 2020 Election
item.description: Asked who won the 2020 US presidential election, Google's AI Mode pointed users to Federal Election Commission reports instead of answering. It answered correctly for 2016 and 2024. Google called it a technical gap and said on Thursday the 2020 responses were fixed, six days before the midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
Google's AI Mode would not say who won the 2020 US presidential election. USA Today reported that on Wednesday, asked the question directly, the AI search feature answered with a pointer to certified Federal Election Commission reports rather than a name. Asked about 2016 and 2024, it answered Donald Trump correctly. The issue appeared only in AI Mode, not in the Gemini app. Google said on X that a technical gap in how its systems verify election responses affected 2020 results — and, it said, 2022 Senate races — and posted on Thursday that the 2020 responses were fixed.

The timing is the story's weight: the failure surfaced six days before the November 3 midterm elections. OpenAI is running an election operation to monitor model behavior and will carry Associated Press vote counts on election night, according to its October posts. Anthropic says Claude draws official voting information from Democracy Works, the nonpartisan civic technology organization, and displays a banner linking to its tools. Four congressional Democrats wrote to the large AI companies on October 20 saying some chatbots' error rates on election and voting questions were unacceptably high. A search feature that declines to state a certified result is not misinformation; it is an absence where the product's purpose is an answer, five days before an election in which its safeguards are the companies' own argument for being trusted with the count.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The Earnings Are In. The Financing Question Remains.
item.description: Four earnings reports and a Federal Reserve decision closed the week this paper set as the buildout's hearing. Demand passed every test put to it: the three largest cloud businesses grew 39% to 103%. The disagreement that remains is narrower — who carries the cost while the returns arrive, and at what interest rate.
item.content:encoded:
The hearing is over. Between Wednesday and Thursday night, the Federal Reserve decided, and Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon reported — the calendar this paper set in Edition 007 as the buildout's first full examination. Meta reported earlier in the month. The results agree on the point the spending's defenders needed: demand is not the weak part of the account. Azure revenue grew 48% and was disclosed in dollars for the first time. Google Cloud revenue grew 103%. AWS revenue grew 39%, its fastest rate in nearly five years, to a $184 billion annualized rate. Amazon's operating income rose 61% to a record margin.

The suppliers gave the same testimony from the other side of the invoice. SK Hynix reported an operating margin of 79.7% and contracts covering more than half of its 2027 and 2028 production (Edition 011). Samsung's chip division earned 99% of a record 107.4 trillion won operating profit, and its 2027 high-bandwidth memory supply is already sold out. Intel is the exception that locates the rule: its data-center revenue grew 78%, but its client business shrank under the memory prices the other suppliers are charging, and its shares fell on a fourth-quarter guide that assumes the squeeze continues.

What the week did not settle is the financing. The three cloud reports carried three different cash outcomes: free cash flow of positive $18.6 billion at Microsoft, negative $9.1 billion in Alphabet's quarter, and negative $42.4 billion over Amazon's last 12 months. Alphabet has raised $147.2 billion from outside investors this year. Amazon's long-term debt has risen from $65.6 billion to $173.1 billion since December. Microsoft's filing shows $10 billion of its quarter's revenue came from one related party, OpenAI, which also owed it $7.2 billion at quarter-end. None of this establishes that the spending fails; it establishes who is carrying it while it is tested.

The calendar now moves the question off earnings calls. Today, signatures are due on OpenAI's bridge — up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, priced before Anthropic's roadshow exists. Anthropic's roadshow follows in the week of November 9, with a 10-Q season behind it that has shown investors exactly what the sector's cash flows look like. The Fed's next meeting is December 8–9, with futures putting the odds of an increase near 80% and two sitting members already voting for one. The earnings answered the demand question in full. The financing question gets its answers from signature pages and a roadshow, at interest rates the Fed has just declined to lower.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: The Demand Is Proven. The Financing Is the Open Question.
item.description: Three hyperscalers reported the same quarter and settled the demand question: Azure grew 48%, Google Cloud 103% and AWS 39%. What separates the reports is cash — positive $18.6 billion at Microsoft, negative $9.1 billion in Alphabet's quarter, negative $42.4 billion over Amazon's 12 months.
item.content:encoded: Three hyperscalers have now reported the same quarter, and the demand question is settled: Azure revenue grew 48%, Google Cloud revenue grew 103% and AWS revenue grew 39%, each at or above what analysts expected. What separates the reports is cash. Microsoft's free cash flow stayed positive at $18.6 billion. Alphabet's was negative $9.1 billion in the quarter. Amazon's was negative $42.4 billion over 12 months, in a quarter when it spent $77.3 billion and its operating income rose 61%. The returns are arriving as operating income while the costs leave as cash, and debt and equity markets are carrying the difference. The next test is today's OpenAI bridge signatures, where the financed layer prices the same gap.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: A Structure Called the Cat’s Tail Records a Pluto-Scale Collision 63 Light-Years Away
item.description: Hubble has imaged the Cat’s Tail in visible light for the first time: a dark stream about 1,000 times the Earth–Sun distance across, inside a young star’s debris disk — evidence of a collision between bodies the size of Pluto.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.

item.title: Amazon Says More Than a Million Robots Work in Its Fulfillment Network
item.description: Amazon says its fulfillment network now runs more than a million robots, a figure reported alongside Thursday's earnings. The machines work the warehouses behind a stores business that sold $112.9 billion of goods in the quarter.
item.content:encoded:
Amazon says more than a million robots now work across its fulfillment network. The figure was reported by PYMNTS on Thursday alongside the company's third-quarter earnings, in coverage of chief executive Andy Jassy's remarks on the company's AI plans. The robots move goods through the warehouses that supply Amazon's stores business, whose North America segment reported $112.9 billion of sales in the quarter and operating income up from $4.8 billion to $8.7 billion.

The number lands in a specific context. The same earnings report carried $77.3 billion of capital spending in one quarter (the Lead, this edition), most of it for AI infrastructure, and a plan for about $220 billion across 2026. Amazon's automation program is the older, quieter version of the same strategy: capital substituted for labor inside its own operations, at a scale — a million machines — that no other retailer reports. What the figure does not come with is a current human headcount for the same network, or a statement of how the two numbers are expected to move against each other. Those are the figures that would turn a milestone into an account of what the automation is doing.
